name: Beriberi traced to a dietary deficiency in Java
summary: Dutch physicians in Java linked beriberi to polished rice, leading to the idea that a missing dietary factor causes disease.
description: In the 1890s Christiaan Eijkman found in Batavia that chickens fed polished rice developed an illness like beriberi and did not when fed unpolished rice. By 1897 the work had led to the conclusion that a substance in rice husk counteracted the disease, and Adolphe Vorderman's report on the prisons of Java and Madura tied beriberi to the type of rice eaten. Gerrit Grijns proposed in 1901 that the disease results from the lack of a natural nutrient that polished rice does not contain.

impact.note: The finding ended beriberi where rice diets were changed and fed into nutrition practice in many societies; it was a new kind of explanation of disease, and the study of vitamins grew from it.

why: Eijkman was given the task of finding the causes of the disease in the Dutch colonies in Asia, and he noticed by chance that hens fed milled rice showed similar symptoms.

evidence.supports: Christian Eijkman in the 1890s in Batavia, Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia), who found that chickens that had developed a beriberi-like illness when fed polished rice, did not do so when they were fed unpolished rice

events.statement: Grijns proposed in 1901 that beriberi results from a lack of a natural nutrient found in unpolished rice.

evidence.supports: In 1901, Grijns proposed that the disease results from the lack of some natural nutrient substance that is found in unpolished rice and in other foods

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The source gives Eijkman's chicken observations only as "in the 1890s"; the same article says he told Vorderman of them in 1895, so they were made by then. A source for the exact year is wanted.
The Nobel page does not say where the 1897 conclusion was reached; EBSCO says Eijkman left Java in 1896, so that event has no place.
Takagi Kanehiro's dietary reform in the Japanese navy (reported by EBSCO under 1887) deserves its own card.
Vorderman's prison figures were not checked against his report.

research.note: EBSCO says Grijns in 1901 "was the first to interpret correctly" the protective substance in rice, as a nutrient whose lack causes the disease; he built on Eijkman's chicken observations of the 1890s and the 1897 conclusion that such a substance exists. Takagi Kanehiro's 1887 dietary explanation, that the navy diet was low in protein, is earlier but is not the idea of a missing trace substance.
